A scatter plot shows how two variables co-vary but hides their *individual* distributions — a top-right cloud can hide one bimodal variable and one skewed one. **Marginal plots** fix this by appending the x-variable's distribution along the top edge and the y-variable's along the right edge (histogram, density or boxplot), so the reader sees the joint relationship and the two marginal distributions in one figure \[1\]. The design is popular in clinical and biological scatter plots — e.g., biomarker correlation panels in oncology papers.

This tutorial builds the layout manually with ggplot2 + patchwork \[2\]. The assembly is fully explicit (which scales, which themes, which margins), version-proof, and transfers directly to any panel arrangement. A note on `ggExtra::ggMarginal()`, the popular one-liner for this design, appears in the callout below.

This tutorial covers two workflows:

1. A scatter plot with marginal histograms;
2. Species-stratified marginal densities with a shared color scale.

## Setup

-   System Requirements: Cross-platform (Linux/MacOS/Windows)

-   Programming language: R

-   Dependent packages: `ggplot2`; `dplyr`; `patchwork`; `palmerpenguins`

```{r packages setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, output=FALSE}
# Installing necessary packages
if (!requireNamespace("palmerpenguins", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("palmerpenguins")
}
if (!requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("patchwork")
}

# Load packages
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{r}
sessioninfo::session_info("attached")
```

## Data Preparation

We use the `penguins` data from the `palmerpenguins` package \[3\]: 344 Antarctic penguins of three species with morphological measurements. Bill length and flipper length are complete for 342 animals — the classic correlation pair for this layout.

```{r load data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data(penguins, package = "palmerpenguins")

peng <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(bill_length_mm), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))
xr <- range(peng$bill_length_mm)
yr <- range(peng$flipper_length_mm)
cat("Rows used:", nrow(peng), "\n")
```

## Visualization

### 1. Scatter with Marginal Histograms

The trick is three plots sharing scales: the main scatter, a top histogram with the *same x scale*, and a right histogram with the *same y scale* (drawn on a reversed x axis so its bars grow toward the scatter). patchwork's `design` string places the three panels.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.1MarginalHist
#| fig-cap: "Scatter of bill length versus flipper length with marginal histograms on both edges; shared scales keep the marginals aligned with the scatter."
#| out.width: "75%"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false

nb <- 28

pmain <- ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2166AC", alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = xr) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = yr) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

ptop <- ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = nb, fill = "#2166AC", alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = xr) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

pright <- ggplot(peng, aes(y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = nb, fill = "#2166AC", alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = yr) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "reverse") +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

design <- "AB
CD"
p1 <- wrap_plots(A = ptop, B = plot_spacer(), C = pmain, D = pright,
                 design = design) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1), heights = c(1, 3))
p1
```

Note the marginal histograms carry information the scatter cannot: flipper length is bimodal even though the scatter looks like one continuous cloud.

### 2. Grouped Marginal Densities

```{r}
#| label: fig-2.1GroupedDensity
#| fig-cap: "Species-stratified scatter and marginal densities: Gentoo separates on both axes, Adelie and Chinstrap overlap in the scatter but differ in bill length (top marginal)."
#| out.width: "75%"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false

pal <- c(Adelie = "#4E79A7", Chinstrap = "#F28E2B", Gentoo = "#E15759")

pmain_g <- ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = xr) + scale_y_continuous(limits = yr) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.72, 0.22), legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "grey80",
                                         linewidth = 0.2))

ptop_g <- ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = xr) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

pright_g <- ggplot(peng, aes(y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = yr) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "reverse") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

p2 <- wrap_plots(A = ptop_g, B = plot_spacer(), C = pmain_g, D = pright_g,
                 design = design) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1), heights = c(1, 3))
p2
```

This is where the layout earns its keep: Adelie and Chinstrap are inseparable on flipper length (right marginal), but the top marginal splits them cleanly on bill length — a fact invisible in the scatter alone.

::: callout-tip
## Practice tips

-   Keep the three panels on **identical scales**: the marginal plot is only honest if its bars line up with the scatter's axes. Freeze limits with `scale_*_continuous(limits = range(...))` in every panel.
-   Reverse the side-panel axis (`scale_x_continuous(trans = "reverse")`) so bars grow toward the scatter — the standard convention.
-   One row of code does this with `ggExtra::ggMarginal(p)` \[1\] — but as of 2026-10 the package's marginal panels collapse under ggplot2 ≥ 4.0 (rendered as black rectangles); if you see that, fall back to the manual assembly above, which is version-proof.
-   For n < ~30, swap histograms for marginal *points/rug* — binned counts of tiny samples mislead.
:::

## Application

Marginal-enhanced scatters appear throughout method-comparison and biomarker papers: correlation of two assays with each assay's distribution on the margins, dose-response panels, and PCA/t-SNE projections with per-axis score distributions. The panel below mirrors a typical publication layout: (A) marginal histograms for the pooled cohort and (B) grouped marginal densities by subpopulation.
